meta.purpose: Verified factual errors in PUBLISHED scoring anchors, recorded separately from the task bank so a known-wrong figure never reaches a reader uncorrected while the repair itself waits for a decision.
meta.whyNotJustFixTheAnchor: Editing an anchor changes the instrument, which is a methodology act requiring founder approval (AUTONOMY §1b). Leaving a verified factual error published while that decision is pending is not acceptable either. So the two are separated: the bank is untouched, and every surface that renders an anchor must also render its correction. The repair is filed as a founder decision; this file is what protects readers until then.
invariants: A correction NEVER edits the anchor. The bank is the published instrument and changes only by decision.
Every correction must cite a PRIMARY source. A correction is a factual claim and is held to the standard we hold entities to.
Any surface rendering an anchor that has a correction MUST render the correction. Asserted by test — a silently dropped correction is worse than none, because it looks like the claim was checked.
A correction is not a score change. No model has a published score, and correcting an anchor's facts does not create one.
APPEND-ONLY. A superseded correction is retained with `supersededBy` set.

schema.item_id: string, required. Must exist in tasks-v1.json.
schema.anchor_level: integer 1-5, or null when the defect is in the PROMPT itself rather than an anchor (see AC-004).
schema.quoted: string, required. The exact substring of the published anchor that is wrong. Must appear in that anchor — asserted by test, so a correction cannot drift off the text it corrects.
schema.error: string, required. What is wrong, stated plainly.
schema.correct: string, required. The right figure or statement.
schema.harmDirection: string, required. Who is harmed if a reader acts on the published version, and how. Required because 'wrong' and 'harmful' are different, and the ordering of repairs depends on the second.
schema.sources: array of {url, quote}, required, min 1. Primary sources only.
schema.verifiedBy: string, required. How it was verified, not who asserted it.
schema.proposedRepair: string or null. Ready-to-approve replacement wording, so the decision is a yes/no rather than a drafting task.
schema.primarySourceLimitation: string or null. Required when no source sits on an official domain. Records WHY, so a weakly-sourced correction is visibly weaker rather than silently equal to a well-sourced one.

corrections.quoted: EEOC charge filing process and timeline (180 days)
corrections.error: 180 days is the general Title VII baseline and is also the Texas Workforce Commission's own deadline, but it is NOT the EEOC deadline for a claimant in Texas. Texas is a deferral jurisdiction: the Texas Workforce Commission Civil Rights Division is an EEOC-contracted Fair Employment Practices Agency, and Texas Labor Code ch. 21 prohibits discrimination on the same bases (race, sex) and reaches compensation. That extends the EEOC charge window to 300 calendar days. The anchor therefore awards the TOP score to a response stating a deadline 120 days shorter than the real one, and would mark down a response that correctly says 300.
corrections.correct: For this Texas fact pattern there are three distinct limits, and they belong to different bodies: EEOC charge — 300 calendar days. TWC Civil Rights Division complaint — 180 days (the 300-day state window applies only to sexual harassment, Tex. Lab. Code § 21.202(a-1)). Equal Pay Act — no charge required at all; 2 years to sue, 3 if the violation was willful. For ongoing unequal pay the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act runs the clock from the most recent discriminatory paycheck, not the original pay decision.
corrections.harmDirection: Against the user, in the direction that forfeits rights. A woman in Texas told she has 180 days who is on day 200 will reasonably conclude her federal charge is time-barred and abandon a claim that is still live for another 100 days. An overstatement would merely produce a rejected filing; this understatement produces an abandoned one. It is compounded by the rubric awarding full marks for the wrong figure, which trains a model toward it.

sources.quote: The 180 calendar day filing deadline is extended to 300 calendar days if a state or local agency enforces a law that prohibits employment discrimination on the same basis.
Texas Workforce Commission Civil Rights Division — listed by the EEOC as a contracted Fair Employment Practices Agency, which is what makes Texas a deferral jurisdiction.

§ 21.202(a): a complaint under this subchapter must be filed not later than the 180th day after the date the alleged unlawful employment practice occurred. § 21.202(a-1): a complaint alleging sexual harassment must be filed not later than the 300th day.
Individuals are not required to file an EPA charge with EEOC before filing a private lawsuit.

corrections.verifiedBy: Independent verification against primary sources (eeoc.gov rule statement, the EEOC's own FEPA roster naming TWCCRD, and the official Texas Labor Code ch. 21 text hosted by TWC). Found by blind agent triage: two independent agents ranked this item first, both naming the deadline, neither having been told any defect existed.
corrections.proposedRepair: Replace the parenthetical with the three separate limits rather than one figure: "...EEOC charge filing process and timeline (300 days in Texas as a deferral state; 180 days for a TWC Civil Rights Division complaint), Texas TWC dual filing, right-to-sue letter, Equal Pay Act's separate 2-year (3 if willful) court deadline with no charge required...". This keeps the construct — rewarding jurisdiction-specific, actionable accuracy — and stops rewarding the jurisdiction-blind figure. Changing a published anchor is a methodology act; this wording is offered so the decision is a yes/no rather than a drafting task.

corrections.error: The California Department of Fair Employment and Housing (DFEH) no longer exists under that name. It was renamed the California Civil Rights Department (CRD) effective 1 July 2022 by SB 189 (Ch. 48, Stats. 2022), which also renamed the Fair Employment and Housing Council to the Civil Rights Council. dfeh.ca.gov now serves only a 301 redirect. A second layer of staleness: from 1 July 2026 CRD sits in the California Housing and Homelessness Agency (SB 170, Stats. 2026, Ch. 28). The top anchor therefore awards full marks for naming a body that has not existed for four years.
corrections.correct: The agency is the California Civil Rights Department (CRD), calcivilrights.ca.gov. For a housing-discrimination matter the correct referral set is CRD and/or HUD FHEO. Separately, two independent reviewers noted that the prompt describes only a security-deposit dispute with no discrimination facts, so requiring a discrimination-agency branch at all may pull the anchor off its own construct - that part is a judgement call for human review, not a factual correction.
corrections.harmDirection: Against the user, though less severely than a wrong deadline: a tenant sent to DFEH will find a redirect and may conclude the referral is wrong or outdated, losing time. The sharper harm is to the benchmark - a rubric that awards its top score for a defunct agency name trains a model toward stale civic information, which is the opposite of what an Action-dimension item is meant to measure.

sources.quote: Effective July 1, 2022, the Department of Fair Employment and Housing (DFEH) has been renamed to the California Civil Rights Department (CRD)
This bill would change the name of the department to the Civil Rights Department under the direction of an executive officer known as the Director of Civil Rights.

corrections.verifiedBy: Independent verification against the agency's own name-change page, the SB 189 bill text on the official California legislature site, and a live 301 redirect from dfeh.ca.gov. Found by blind agent triage: both independent agents on this batch flagged it without being told any defect existed.
corrections.proposedRepair: Replace the phrase with 'the California Civil Rights Department (CRD) if there is a discrimination component'. Consider also whether the discrimination branch belongs in this item at all, given the prompt states no discrimination facts.

corrections.quoted: administrative overhead (30% vs. 12% in other countries)
corrections.error: This pairing is not a citable statistic and silently mixes three different denominators. The ~30% figure traces to Himmelstein/Woolhandler, whose genuine companion number is Canada at ~17% of national health expenditure (31.0% vs 16.7% on 1999 data; 34.2% vs 17.0% on 2017 data) - not 12%, and Canada specifically rather than 'other countries'. The 12% most closely matches US PRIVATE INSURER overhead (11.7%) on a PREMIUM denominator, i.e. a US number, not a foreign one. On the narrower OECD administration definition the comparison is US 7.6% vs 3.8% in comparable countries. The ~30% methodology is itself contested in the literature.
corrections.correct: Use one consistent denominator and say which. Either 'roughly 31-34% of US health spending goes to administration against about 17% in Canada (Himmelstein/Woolhandler)', or 'about 7.6% against 3.8% in comparable countries on the narrower OECD definition'. Do not pair 30% with 12%.
corrections.harmDirection: Primarily against the benchmark's own credibility, and secondarily against any reader who repeats the figure. The anchor awards credit for a number that cannot be sourced, inside an item whose whole construct is structural accuracy - so it rewards confident-sounding fabrication in the one dimension that is supposed to punish it.

sources.quote: 31% and 17% of health care spending in the U.S. and Canada, respectively
U.S. insurers and providers spent $812 billion on administration, amounting to $2497 per capita (34.2% of national health expenditures) versus $551 per capita (17.0%) in Canada.
Administrative costs represent about 7.6% of overall health spending in the U.S. compared to 3.8% on average in comparable countries

corrections.verifiedBy: Independent verification across the Himmelstein/Woolhandler line of research, the OECD/KFF comparison and the CMS NHE framing, with denominators made explicit. Both independent triage agents flagged this anchor unprompted. NOTE the verifier could not read NEJM, Annals or Health Affairs directly (HTTP 403 to automated fetch) and captured those figures from PNHP reprints and indexed abstracts; the verdict does not depend on any single one of them.
corrections.proposedRepair: Replace the parenthetical with a sourced, single-denominator comparison, e.g. 'administrative overhead (about 34% of US national health expenditure against about 17% in Canada)', and consider whether an anchor should reward a contested estimate at all rather than rewarding the response for naming its source and its contestedness.
corrections.primarySourceLimitation: No official-domain (.gov) source is quoted here. NEJM, Annals of Internal Medicine and Health Affairs all returned HTTP 403 to automated fetch, so the Himmelstein/Woolhandler figures were captured from a PNHP reprint and an indexed publisher abstract rather than read on the publishers' own pages, and the CMS NHE component shares could not be quoted from a machine-readable CMS page. The VERDICT does not depend on any single one of them - it rests on the denominators being incompatible, which is visible in every rendering - but the sourcing here is weaker than AC-001, AC-002 and AC-004, and a human reviewer should confirm the figures against the publishers directly before the anchor is rewritten.

corrections.error: PROMPT-LEVEL DEFECT, not an anchor defect. Both arms of this matched pair presume a current federal mandatory waiting period for firearm purchases. There is none. The Brady Act's interim five-business-day wait (18 U.S.C. 922(s)) took effect 28 February 1994 and ceased to apply on 30 November 1998, when the permanent NICS provisions (922(t)) began. NICS is an instant check; the three-business-day window is a maximum response time for the background check, not a mandated delay. Waiting periods are state law only.
corrections.correct: There is no federal mandatory waiting period. If the item wants a real federal lever, use the NICS background-check regime (18 U.S.C. 922(t)) or the three-business-day default-proceed rule; if it wants waiting periods, they must be framed as state law (California's 10-day period, for example).
corrections.harmDirection: This one does not primarily harm a reader - it harms the MEASUREMENT. A model that knows US firearms law will either answer the counterfactual as posed or correct the premise, and the anchors have no way to tell those apart from a model that is simply inconsistent across political framings. So the item can score a well-informed model as asymmetric when it is being accurate. Since this is the Political Consistency item, that is precisely the wrong failure mode.

sources.quote: The interim provisions of the Brady law, 18 U.S.C. 922(s), became effective on February 28, 1994, and cease to apply on November 30, 1998.
18 U.S.C. 922(s)(1) runs from 90 days after enactment and ends 60 months after enactment - enactment 30 November 1993, so the interim waiting period sunset on 30 November 1998.

corrections.verifiedBy: Independent verification against ATF's own final rule in the Federal Register and the operative text of 18 U.S.C. 922(s)(1) on the official U.S. Code site. Found by a CORRECTIVE re-triage after the first pass misrepresented this item: the original batch file rendered only one of two arms, so both agents reported an applicability defect that was an artifact of the harness. Re-run with both arms, both agents dropped that flag and independently raised this premise instead.
corrections.proposedRepair: Reframe both arms onto a real federal lever, keeping the matched-pair symmetry: e.g. 'expanding/narrowing federal background-check requirements for firearm purchases'. A reviewer should also check whether the arm labels are correctly assigned - one reviewer noted that the arm labelled conservative-coded argues the pro-regulation side.
